content: Blood plasma is the liquid portion of blood in which blood cells are suspended. It constitutes approximately 55% of the total blood volume. Blood plasma can be obtained by placing a sample of fresh blood in a centrifuge, which separates the blood cells from the plasma by spinning the sample until the cells settle at the bottom of the tube. The plasma is then either poured off or drawn out. A medical procedure known as plasmapheresis involves separating plasma from red blood cells for therapeutic purposes. Blood plasma contains several essential proteins, including fibrinogen (a key clotting factor), globulins, and human serum albumin. Occasionally, plasma may contain viral contaminants, which must be removed through specialized viral processing techniques. Plasma is a clear fluid with a pale yellow hue and is primarily composed of water, blood proteins, and inorganic electrolytes. Plasma also functions as a transport medium for various substances, including glucose, lipids, amino acids, hormones, metabolic waste products, carbon dioxide (CO2), and oxygen (O2). However, the oxygen transport capacity of plasma is significantly lower than that of hemoglobin in red blood cells. Under hyperbaric conditions, the carbon dioxide content in plasma increases. Plasma also serves as a storage and transport medium for clotting factors. Blood serum, in contrast, is plasma from which clotting factors have been removed, a process achieved by allowing fresh blood to clot before centrifugation. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is derived from a single unit of blood collected from an individual donor. After collection, it is frozen and can be stored for up to one year. FFP retains all the coagulation factors and proteins present in the original blood sample. It is commonly used to treat coagulopathies, such as those caused by warfarin overdose, liver disease, or dilutional coagulopathy. If FFP is stored beyond the standard time frame, it is reclassified as frozen plasma, which is similar but no longer contains fully viable coagulation factors. FFP is also used in the treatment of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), as platelet transfusion is not a viable treatment option for this condition. Dried plasma was first developed and utilized during World War II. Before the United States entered the war, liquid plasma and whole blood were the primary forms used. The Blood for Britain program in the early 1940s, which aimed to supply plasma to Britain, was highly successful and gained widespread support in the United States. Dr. Charles Drew played a pivotal role in this effort, serving as the medical supervisor of the Plasma for Britain project. He revolutionized blood collection and processing by transforming laboratory-scale methods into the first successful mass production techniques. However, the military decided to develop a dried plasma product for the armed forces to simplify transportation, packaging, and storage while reducing the risk of breakage. The resulting Army-Navy dried plasma package consisted of two tin cans containing 400 cc bottles. One bottle held distilled water, while the other contained dried plasma. The plasma could be reconstituted in about three minutes and remained usable for approximately four hours. Following the success of the Plasma for Britain project, Dr. Drew was appointed director of the Red Cross blood bank and assistant director of the National Research Council, overseeing blood collection for the U.S. Army and Navy. Dr. Drew strongly opposed the military's policy of segregating blood and plasma donations by the race of the donor, arguing that there were no racial differences in human blood. He warned that this policy would result in unnecessary deaths, as soldiers and sailors might be forced to wait for same-race blood. By the end of World War II, the American Red Cross had supplied enough blood to produce over six million plasma packages. Much of the surplus plasma was returned to the United States for civilian use. During the Korean War, serum albumin replaced dried plasma for use in combat settings.
